Importing In-House & Custom Data

custom_data.Rmd
library(omiprep)

Who this vignette is for

omiprep ships dedicated readers for four commercial platforms — read_metabolon(), read_nightingale(), read_olink() and read_somalogic(). Those readers exist only to translate a vendor’s particular spreadsheet layout into a common structure. They are a convenience, not a requirement.

If your data were generated in-house, come from a platform without a dedicated reader, or have already been through an upstream pipeline, you can build an Omiprep object directly from flat text files. Everything downstream — quality_control(), summarise(), generate_report(), export() — then behaves identically, because all the readers do is produce the same three tables you will assemble here by hand.

The three tables

An Omiprep object is built from exactly three pieces:

Piece Shape Requirement
data numeric matrix, samples in rows, features in columns rownames are sample ids, colnames are feature ids
samples data.frame, one row per sample must contain a column named sample_id
features data.frame, one row per feature must contain a column named feature_id

Beyond those two id columns, both metadata tables are free-form: add as many annotation columns as you like (batch, run order, sex, age, pathway, assay panel, LOD), or none at all. omiprep carries them through QC and reporting untouched.

Are the column names strict?

Yes. sample_id and feature_id are matched exactly and are case-sensitive. There is no automatic mapping or fuzzy matching: Sample_ID, sampleID and SampleId are all rejected, with an error naming the column it expected.

This is a deliberate design choice — silently guessing which of a user’s columns holds the identifier is a good way to mis-assign an entire dataset. Conforming is a one-line rename, shown below.

A worked example from flat text files

The package bundles a small example dataset as three plain CSV files, in exactly the form an in-house pipeline might produce them.

pkg <- "omiprep"
data_file     <- system.file("extdata", "dummy_data.csv",     package = pkg)
samples_file  <- system.file("extdata", "dummy_samples.csv",  package = pkg)
features_file <- system.file("extdata", "dummy_features.csv", package = pkg)

1) Read the measurement matrix

The measurement table has sample ids in the first column and feature ids as headers. Read it with row.names = 1 and coerce to a matrix. check.names = FALSE keeps feature ids exactly as written — without it, R prefixes purely numeric column names with X.

data <- as.matrix(read.csv(data_file, row.names = 1, check.names = FALSE))

dim(data)
#> [1] 125 253
data[1:4, 1:3]
#>           48719    43532      46639
#> sam_1 1.5376548       NA 0.26359902
#> sam_2 1.8382935       NA 0.07758324
#> sam_3        NA 1.147501         NA
#> sam_4 0.9071567 7.172319 0.41313486

For a tab-delimited file, use read.delim() instead; nothing else changes.

2) Read the sample and feature metadata 

samples  <- read.csv(samples_file,  row.names = 1, check.names = FALSE)
features <- read.csv(features_file, row.names = 1, check.names = FALSE)

names(samples)
#>  [1] "sample_id"         "parent_sample_id"  "client_identifier"
#>  [4] "sex"               "age"               "bmi"              
#>  [7] "LC/MS Polar"       "LC/MS Neg"         "LC/MS Pos Early"  
#> [10] "LC/MS Pos Late"
names(features)
#>  [1] "feature_id"        "pathway_sortorder" "biochemical"      
#>  [4] "super_pathway"     "sub_pathway"       "comp_id"          
#>  [7] "platform"          "chemical_id"       "ri"               
#> [10] "mass"              "cas"               "pubchem"          
#> [13] "kegg"              "group_hmdb"

Both tables already carry the required id columns alongside their annotation.

head(samples[, c("sample_id", "sex", "age", "bmi")], 3)
#>   sample_id  sex age   bmi
#> 1     sam_1 male  50 17.09
#> 2     sam_2 male  42 27.33
#> 3     sam_3 male  43 30.56
head(features[, c("feature_id", "biochemical", "super_pathway")], 3)
#>       feature_id   biochemical super_pathway
#> 48719      48719     X - 23145          <NA>
#> 43532      43532 veratric acid   Xenobiotics
#> 46639      46639     X - 12851          <NA>

3) Build the object 

mydata <- Omiprep(data = data, samples = samples, features = features)

summary(mydata)
#> Omiprep Object Summary
#> --------------------------
#> Samples      : 125
#> Features     : 253
#> Data Layers  : 1
#> Layer Names  : input
#> 
#> Sample Summary Layers : none
#> Feature Summary Layers: none
#> 
#> Sample Annotation (metadata):
#>   Columns: 10
#>   Names  : sample_id, parent_sample_id, client_identifier, sex, age, bmi, LC/MS Polar, LC/MS Neg, LC/MS Pos Early, LC/MS Pos Late
#> 
#> Feature Annotation (metadata):
#>   Columns: 14
#>   Names  : feature_id, pathway_sortorder, biochemical, super_pathway, sub_pathway, comp_id, platform, chemical_id, ri, mass, cas, pubchem, kegg, group_hmdb
#> 
#> Exclusion Codes Summary:
#> 
#>   Sample Exclusions:
#> Exclusion | Count
#> -----------------
#> user_excluded                     | 0
#> extreme_sample_missingness        | 0
#> user_defined_sample_missingness   | 0
#> user_defined_sample_totalpeakarea | 0
#> user_defined_sample_pca_outlier   | 0
#> 
#>   Feature Exclusions:
#> Exclusion | Count
#> -----------------
#> user_excluded                    | 0
#> extreme_feature_missingness      | 0
#> user_defined_feature_missingness | 0
#> user_defined_feature_skewness    | 0

That is the whole import. From here the object is indistinguishable from one produced by read_metabolon().

Renaming your own columns

If your files use different identifier names, rename them before constructing the object:

# a metadata table as an in-house pipeline might label it
inhouse <- data.frame(
  SampleName = samples$sample_id,
  RunBatch   = samples$`LC/MS Polar`
)

names(inhouse)[names(inhouse) == "SampleName"] <- "sample_id"
names(inhouse)
#> [1] "sample_id" "RunBatch"

The helper clean_names() is useful when your headers contain spaces, dots, dashes or percent signs. It lowercases and standardises them, which turns a header like Sample ID into sample_id directly:

clean_names(c("Sample ID", "Feature-Name.1", "Concentration %"))
#> [1] "sample_id"         "featurename_1"     "concentration_pct"

Note that clean_names() lowercases everything, so apply it to the whole header vector rather than to one column, and check the result before relying on it.

Identifier types: a common pitfall

Matrix dimnames in R are always character. If your ids are numeric and you read the metadata without specifying types, read.csv() will type them as integer, and the ids will not compare equal to the matrix names.

Omiprep() guards against this by coercing sample_id and feature_id to character for you, so the naive read used above works. If you assemble metadata by some other route, it is still worth being explicit:

features <- read.csv(features_file, colClasses = c(feature_id = "character"))

The ids must match the matrix names as a set; order does not matter. The constructor reorders both metadata tables to follow the matrix, carrying all annotation columns with them. Any id present in the matrix but absent from the metadata is an error, and the message names the offending ids.

A minimal object

Annotation is optional. If you have nothing but a matrix, generate the two id columns from its dimnames:

minimal <- Omiprep(
  data     = data,
  samples  = data.frame(sample_id  = rownames(data)),
  features = data.frame(feature_id = colnames(data))
)

dim(minimal@data)
#> [1] 125 253   1

Running the pipeline

Everything downstream now works as documented elsewhere. Quality control:

mydata <- quality_control(
  mydata,
  source_layer        = "input",
  sample_missingness  = 0.2,
  feature_missingness = 0.2,
  cores               = 2
)
#>                         step seconds   pct
#>                   validation    0.00   0.0
#>                summarise_raw    1.80  33.8
#>                   copy_layer    0.00   0.0
#>   extreme_sample_missingness    0.00   0.0
#>  extreme_feature_missingness    0.00   0.0
#>           sample_missingness    0.00   0.0
#>          total_sum_abundance    0.01   0.2
#>                summarise_pca    1.68  31.5
#>              summarise_final    1.60  30.0
#>                        total    5.33 100.1
summary(mydata)
#> Omiprep Object Summary
#> --------------------------
#> Samples      : 125
#> Features     : 253
#> Data Layers  : 2
#> Layer Names  : input, qc
#> 
#> Sample Summary Layers : input, qc
#> Feature Summary Layers: input, qc
#> 
#> Sample Annotation (metadata):
#>   Columns: 12
#>   Names  : sample_id, parent_sample_id, client_identifier, sex, age, bmi, LC/MS Polar, LC/MS Neg, LC/MS Pos Early, LC/MS Pos Late, reason_excluded, excluded
#> 
#> Feature Annotation (metadata):
#>   Columns: 16
#>   Names  : feature_id, pathway_sortorder, biochemical, super_pathway, sub_pathway, comp_id, platform, chemical_id, ri, mass, cas, pubchem, kegg, group_hmdb, reason_excluded, excluded
#> 
#> Exclusion Codes Summary:
#> 
#>   Sample Exclusions:
#> Exclusion | Count
#> -----------------
#> user_excluded                     | 0
#> extreme_sample_missingness        | 0
#> user_defined_sample_missingness   | 1
#> user_defined_sample_totalpeakarea | 0
#> user_defined_sample_pca_outlier   | 0
#> 
#>   Feature Exclusions:
#> Exclusion | Count
#> -----------------
#> user_excluded                    |  0
#> extreme_feature_missingness      |  5
#> user_defined_feature_missingness | 46
#> user_defined_feature_skewness    |  0

Note that total_sum_abundance_sd assumes features share a comparable abundance scale. For in-house data that has already been normalised, standardised, or combined across assays, set it to NA to skip that step, as total abundance across such features is not interpretable.
